chips.label: What does Eric do?
answer: Eric is a Principal Design Engineer in Denver. He works on design systems, agentic engineering workflows, and front-end platforms across React, Angular, and Vue.
He describes himself as a team-focused UI/UX creative who provides the design and development services an organization runs on day to day.

chips.label: What is he working on now?
answer: Since December 2023 he has been a Senior UX Engineer at CoBank, where he leads the design system: the Figma UI kit and tokens, the React and Material UI component library, and the Storybook pipeline that connects them.
He also builds agentic tooling there, including an MCP server that turns Figma specs into token-wired React scaffolding and a CI/CD check that catches UI drift before merge.

chips.label: How does he build design systems?
answer: He starts in Figma with the brand style guide, UI kit, and design tokens, then carries the same tokens into code so design and engineering share one source.
Examples: a React and Material UI system serving 120+ developers and designers at CoBank, a Vue.js component library in Storybook at Health Scholars, and a VR design system in Unity UI Toolkit.

chips.label: How does he use AI agents in his work?
answer: At CoBank he built an MCP server and agent toolkit that turns Figma specs into token-wired React scaffolding, cutting feature development time by 40 %.
He also added an agentic spec and drift detection step to CI/CD that catches UI inconsistencies before merge, cutting drift fixes by 33 %.

chips.label: How does he approach accessibility?
answer: He builds accessibility into the components themselves. At CoBank he standardized component access and implementation guidelines, which dropped performance and accessibility errors by 37 %.
Earlier, he built an inclusive pattern library and front end for the Denver Museum of Nature & Science.

chips.label: What is his design process?
answer: His work runs through design discovery, visual design, prototyping, and front-end development, so he can take an idea from research to working code.
He prototypes in Figma, Sketch, and HTML, and has led design sprints and interface workshops for engineering, VR, and product marketing teams.

chips.label: How does he get from Figma to code?
answer: Through tokens. His pipeline syncs Figma variables to JSON tokens, then to Material UI themes and Storybook in one pass, so a design change reaches the component library without hand copying.
On top of that, his agent toolkit generates React scaffolding already wired to those tokens.

chips.label: What is he like to work with?
answer: He is team-focused. He works with cross-functional department leaders to identify and resolve issues, prioritize projects, and provide a high level of service.
At Health Scholars he led design sprints and VR interface training for the web, VR, and marketing teams.

chips.label: How long has he been doing this?
answer: Since 2003. He started in post-production and multimedia in San Diego and at the Defense Language Institute, then moved into UI design and front-end development at The Navigators.

From there he worked independently for startups and clients like the Denver Museum of Nature & Science, spent over five years at Health Scholars on web and VR products, consulted for Threecolts, and joined CoBank in 2023.

chips.label: What tools and frameworks does he use?
answer: In code: HTML, SCSS, JavaScript, and TypeScript; React, Vue.js, and Angular; Storybook; Bootstrap, Foundation, and Tailwind; AWS, GraphQL, and Hasura; and Hugo, WordPress, and Kentico.
In design and delivery: Figma, Sketch, Adobe CC, Git, CodePen, Jira, and Trello.

chips.label: Has he designed for VR?
answer: Yes. At Health Scholars he designed brand and UI systems for 6 web applications and 10 VR simulation products, including the Workbench developer platform.
He also set up a VR design system in Unity UI Toolkit that sped up 3D prototyping.

chips.label: Where did he study?
answer: Platt College in San Diego: an A.A.S. in Graphic Design in 2003 and a B.S. in Media Arts in 2005.

chips.label: How can I reach him?
answer: Email is the best way. You can also find him on LinkedIn, GitHub, and CodePen, or read the full résumé.
